rabbitHoles.title: Trauma, Freeze & Somatic Work
rabbitHoles.centralQuestion: What if trauma is something the body is still doing, not just something that happened?
rabbitHoles.shortIntro: This started with experience, not theory. Something happened in my body that I couldn't explain, so I went looking for models that could.
rabbitHoles.currentTake: I think my nervous system gradually came out of a long freeze response. Repressed emotion and the completion of things my body could not do at the time seem central to what happened. I don't know how much was healing and how much was symptom management. That question is still open.

blocks.heading: Why I went down this rabbit hole
blocks.body: When I was 16, I was in a car crash. Years later, during a very intense period of self-directed somatic work, my body began moving in ways that felt connected to an interrupted protective response from that accident. There was shaking, emotion, dry heaving, and a lot I did not consciously direct. Cannabis made bodily information accessible in a way analysis had not. Whether every interpretation I made was correct is a separate question. The experience itself was impossible for me to ignore.

blocks.heading: The model that made sense of it
blocks.body: Peter Levine's work gave me a useful frame: threat responses can remain incomplete, and the body may keep trying to finish them. Somatic Experiencing uses sensation, small doses of activation, and movement rather than treating trauma as only a story to understand. I have not worked formally with a Somatic Experiencing practitioner. I read Levine and used parts of the model in my own exploration.

blocks.heading: Other tools that became part of the trail
blocks.body: No single framework explains the whole thing for me.
items: IFS and parts language have been useful in self-sessions and relationships.
Applied neurology and nerve work have sometimes been practically useful.
Breathwork helps change state; my current simple version is 4 seconds in and 6 seconds out.
Biofield Tuning may have been a catalyst in the larger process, though I don't know the mechanism.

blocks.heading: The question I keep coming back to
blocks.body: What is actually healing, and what is just symptom management? I think I have more capacity than I did before. I also think some things I called healing may have been temporary relief or a new explanation laid over the same problem. I don't have a clean answer.

rabbitHoles.title: Light Biology
rabbitHoles.centralQuestion: Is light doing much more than letting us see and making vitamin D?
rabbitHoles.shortIntro: This rabbit hole starts with the body clock and keeps getting stranger: spectrum, red and near-infrared light, mitochondria, biophotons, and the possibility that light is part of how living systems organize themselves.
rabbitHoles.currentTake: I'm quite convinced that the light environment matters far beyond vitamin D. Circadian timing is the solid foundation. Red and near-infrared light can clearly move physiology through mitochondrial and signaling chemistry. I also think biophotons may be another channel living systems use to coordinate, but detecting the glow is the easy part. Showing that cells actually use it to make collective decisions is the experiment that still needs doing.

blocks.heading: Bright days. Dark nights.
blocks.body: The least strange part is already powerful. Light is a timing signal. Morning and daytime light help set the clock; artificial light at night can push it the wrong way. The exact effect depends on intensity, timing, spectrum, duration, previous light exposure, and the person. 'Blue light is bad' is too crude. Bright blue-enriched light can be useful during the day and disruptive at the wrong time.

blocks.heading: What I actually do
blocks.body: I try to see outdoor light early, walk outside a lot, get sensible full-body midday sun without burning, and make night darker. I almost never wear sunglasses. I use amber blue-blocking glasses for at least an hour before bed, turn my phone red, and use a sleep mask when a room isn't dark. Those practices belong in Human; this page is the trail behind them.

blocks.heading: Detection isn't communication
blocks.body: Photobiomodulation can begin as local chemistry and still become system-level. Red and near-infrared light can change mitochondrial activity, ATP, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, and downstream signaling. The more interesting question for me is whether those changes alter the collective decision a tissue is making—its electrical state, coupling, repair program, or target pattern—or only change a local metabolic setpoint. Living tissue also emits ultraweak photons, mostly associated with oxidative and mitochondrial activity. That emission can be a useful readout without necessarily being a language. I think cells will use whatever physics is available—ions, forces, chemicals, and perhaps photons—to stay organized. But the existence of photons does not yet show that they form a coherent, body-wide messaging code.

blocks.heading: The experiment I want to see
blocks.body: Can changing an optical signal make distant cells change what they are trying to build, repair, or maintain—not just their ROS or metabolic activity? Can the signal be read, rewritten, blocked, and used to produce a predictable system-level change? That is the causal standard that makes bioelectricity so interesting. If biophotons can hold pattern memory, help resolve an anatomical error, or bind cells into a larger problem-solving unit, they may be another kind of physiological software. If not, the glow may still be an informative metabolic exhaust. I lean toward light being more organizational than the standard story allows, but I don't think that larger claim has been demonstrated yet.

rabbitHoles.title: The Biofield
rabbitHoles.centralQuestion: Is the biofield a real part of physiology—and if it is, what exactly is it?
rabbitHoles.shortIntro: I don't think a person ends at the skin. I think there is a real field-level layer to human physiology, and Biofield Tuning gave me a way to explore it directly. The mechanism is much less settled for me than the phenomenon.
rabbitHoles.currentTake: I believe the biofield is real, extends several feet around the body, and contains or gives access to a person's history. I think it helps organize physiology. I also think coherent sound can interact with distortions in that field. I'm less certain about exactly how it works, how permanent changes are, and how much conscious participation is required.

blocks.heading: What I mean by biofield
blocks.body: I mean a field-level aspect of a living person: electrical, electromagnetic, acoustic, informational, or something our current categories do not describe very well. Eileen Day McKusick describes a plasma-like field several feet around the body, with distortions that correspond to a person's history. That map sounds unusual. In sessions, I have repeatedly found it surprisingly accurate.

blocks.heading: Why I take it seriously
blocks.body: I received roughly fifteen Biofield Tuning sessions, studied McKusick's work extensively, paid practitioners to teach me informally, and began practicing on other people. I have seen people become very relaxed, feel unexpectedly light or euphoric, remember things, and make meaningful life changes afterward. Those experiences are why I think something real is happening. They do not tell me which explanation is correct.

blocks.heading: Four different questions
blocks.body: I try not to collapse these into one answer.
items: Do controlled studies find effects beyond attention, expectation, sound, rest, and context?
Can a relevant field or signal be measured reliably?
Does the proposed biofield map explain what happens in a session?

blocks.heading: What I still don't know
blocks.body: I don't know whether the tuning fork is changing a field, changing attention and nervous-system state, creating a useful ritual, or doing several things at once. I don't know how permanent a session is without the person consciously changing anything. I still think the field is the most interesting place to look.
